courses.title: Beginner Fundamentals
courses.description: The board, square names, and how each piece moves.

lessons.title: Board Basics
lessons.summary: Learn the board, files, ranks, and square names.

steps.title: The board
steps.body: Chess uses 64 squares. Columns are files a through h, left to right for White. Rows are ranks 1 through 8, counting up from White's side.

steps.title: Corners and the center
steps.body: a1 is White's left corner and h1 is White's right corner. The center is d4, e4, d5, and e5.

steps.title: Find the center
steps.body: Click d4, e4, d5, and e5.
steps.successText: Those four squares are the center.
steps.errorText: The center is where the d and e files cross ranks 4 and 5.

steps.title: Name e4
steps.body: File e is the fifth file. Rank 4 is four squares up from White. Click e4.
steps.successText: e4 sits in front of White's king pawn.
steps.errorText: Count a, b, c, d, e, then stop on rank 4.

steps.title: What color is a1?
steps.question: White's left corner, a1, is which color?
steps.successText: a1 is dark. h1, White's right corner, is light.
steps.errorText: Look at a1 again. It is the dark corner.

steps.title: Lesson recap
steps.body: Name a square with its file, then its rank: e4, d5, h1. You will use those names in every lesson.

steps.title: Pieces move differently
steps.body: Rooks slide on ranks and files. Bishops slide on diagonals. The queen does both. Knights jump in an L. Kings step one square. Pawns step forward and capture diagonally.

steps.title: The rook
steps.body: A rook moves any number of empty squares along a rank or file. It cannot jump.

steps.title: Move the rook
steps.body: Move the rook from d4 to d7.
steps.successText: Rooks travel in straight lines.
steps.errorText: Slide the rook straight up the d-file to d7.

steps.title: The bishop
steps.body: A bishop stays on one color and moves any number of empty squares diagonally.

steps.title: Move the bishop
steps.body: Move the bishop from d4 to g7.
steps.successText: That diagonal is the bishop's road.
steps.errorText: Follow the diagonal from d4 to e5, f6, and g7.

steps.title: The knight
steps.body: A knight jumps in an L: two squares one way and one square sideways. It can jump over pieces.

steps.title: Jump the knight
steps.body: Move the knight from d4 to f5.
steps.successText: Two up and one to the side. That is the knight.
steps.errorText: From d4, the L to f5 is two squares toward f and one square up.

steps.title: Move the queen
steps.body: The queen combines rook and bishop. Move her from d4 to h4.
steps.successText: The queen can use any clear rank, file, or diagonal.
steps.errorText: Slide the queen along the fourth rank to h4.

steps.title: Step with the king
steps.body: The king moves one square at a time. Move the white king from e4 to e5.
steps.successText: Kings are slow. Keep yours safe until the endgame.
steps.errorText: The king on e4 can step one square forward to e5.

steps.title: The pawn's first step
steps.body: Pawns move forward. On their first move they may advance one or two squares. Play e2 to e4.
steps.successText: That pawn now controls d5 and f5.
steps.errorText: Push the pawn on e2 two squares to e4.

steps.title: Pawns capture diagonally
steps.body: A pawn cannot capture straight ahead. Capture the black pawn by moving from d4 to e5.
steps.successText: Pawns capture one square diagonally forward.
steps.errorText: Move the white pawn from d4 to e5.

steps.title: Which piece can jump?
steps.question: Which piece can leap over other pieces?
steps.successText: Only the knight jumps. Everyone else needs a clear path.
steps.errorText: Think of the piece that moves in an L.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Check means the king is attacked. The side in check must escape on the next move: move the king, capture the attacker, or block the attack.

steps.title: Lesson recap
steps.body: Learn the shape of each move before you try to attack. A legal move never leaves your own king in check.

steps.title: Why the center matters
steps.body: Pieces in the center reach more squares. A knight in the center has eight jumps. A knight in the corner has two.

steps.title: Mark the center
steps.body: Click the four center squares again: d4, e4, d5, and e5.
steps.successText: Fight for these squares in the opening.
steps.errorText: Stay on d4, e4, d5, and e5.

steps.title: Put a pawn in the center
steps.body: Move the e-pawn from e2 to e4.
steps.successText: e4 claims space and opens a path for the bishop and queen.
steps.errorText: Advance the pawn on e2 to e4.

steps.title: A useful first pawn move
steps.question: Which pawn move fights for the center?
steps.successText: e4 and d4 are the classic central pawn moves.
steps.errorText: Edge pawns do not control d4, e4, d5, or e5.

steps.title: Lesson recap
steps.body: Use your first moves to influence the center. You do not have to capture there. Standing on it, or attacking it, is enough.

courses.title: Opening Principles
courses.description: Fight for the center, develop pieces, and castle.

lessons.title: Opening Goals
lessons.summary: Learn the main goals of the opening.

steps.title: Three opening goals
steps.body: In the first ten moves, do three things: influence the center, develop knights and bishops, and castle your king. Do not hunt the enemy queen.

steps.title: Choose a first move
steps.question: Which move best matches those goals?

choices.label: Na3, putting a knight on the rim

steps.successText: e4 fights for the center and frees the light-squared bishop.
steps.errorText: Start with the center, not the edge and not the queen.

steps.title: Play a principled first move
steps.body: Play one of these: e4, d4, c4, or Nf3.
steps.successText: That move develops a piece or fights for the center.
steps.errorText: Try e2-e4, d2-d4, c2-c4, or the knight from g1 to f3.

steps.title: After 1. e4
steps.body: The pawn on e4 controls d5 and f5. The bishop on f1 and the queen on d1 now have diagonals.

steps.title: Lesson recap
steps.body: Center, development, king safety. If a move does none of those, look for a better one.

steps.title: Develop before you attack
steps.body: Bring knights and bishops out before the queen and rooks. A developed piece influences the board. A piece on its home square does not.

steps.title: Knights like the center
steps.body: Both sides have a pawn in the center. White's next useful job is to develop the knight from g1.

steps.title: Develop the knight
steps.body: Move the knight from g1 to f3. It attacks e5 and prepares castling.
steps.successText: Nf3 develops with a purpose: it eyes the center.
steps.errorText: Move the knight on g1 to f3.

steps.title: Leave the queen at home
steps.question: Why should beginners delay queen moves?

choices.label: The queen is not allowed to move early
Early queen moves lose time when the opponent attacks her
The queen cannot move until a pawn has captured

steps.successText: Develop minor pieces first. The queen joins once she has a clear job.
steps.errorText: The queen is legal early. She just becomes a target.

steps.title: Lesson recap
steps.body: Develop knights toward the center, then bishops, then castle. Rooks belong on open or half-open files later.

lessons.title: King Safety
lessons.summary: Learn why king safety comes early.

steps.title: Castle early
steps.body: Castling moves the king away from the center and brings a rook toward the action. You may castle once per game, and only if the king and that rook have not moved.

steps.title: Ready to castle
steps.body: The knight and the light-squared bishop are out. The squares between the king and the h1 rook are empty.

steps.title: Castle kingside
steps.body: Move the king from e1 to g1. The rook will jump to f1.
steps.successText: The king is safer, and the rook has entered the game.
steps.errorText: Slide the king two squares toward the rook, from e1 to g1.

steps.title: When castling is illegal
steps.question: Which condition stops you from castling?

choices.label: Your king is in check and stays on an attacked square
You have already moved a pawn

steps.successText: You also cannot castle through check, out of check, or if the king or rook has moved.
steps.errorText: Pawn moves do not by themselves cancel castling. Check does.

steps.title: Lesson recap
steps.body: Castle before you attack. A king left on e1 is a target once the center opens.

courses.title: Basic Tactics
courses.description: Forks, pins, and pieces left hanging.

lessons.title: Forks
lessons.summary: Learn how one move can attack two targets.

steps.title: One move, two targets
steps.body: A fork is a move that attacks two pieces at once. The opponent can usually save only one. Knights are famous for forks because their L-shaped jump is hard to see.

steps.title: A knight fork
steps.body: The knight on c7 attacks the king on a8 and the rook on e8 at the same time.

steps.title: Fork the king and queen
steps.body: Move the knight from d4 to f5. It will check the king and attack the queen.
steps.successText: f5 attacks g7 and e3. That is a fork.
steps.errorText: Jump the knight from d4 to f5.

steps.title: A pawn fork
steps.body: Push the pawn from d2 to d4. From d4 it attacks both black knights.
steps.successText: Pawns fork on the two squares they attack diagonally.
steps.errorText: Advance the d2 pawn two squares to d4.

steps.title: Spot the idea
steps.question: What makes a fork powerful?

choices.label: It attacks two things, so one can be won
It lets a pawn move backward

steps.successText: Look for one piece that can attack two undefended or valuable targets.
steps.errorText: A fork is about two targets, not an automatic mate.

steps.title: Lesson recap
steps.body: Before you move, ask: does my opponent have a fork? After you move, ask the same question about your own pieces.

lessons.title: Pins
lessons.summary: Learn how pinned pieces lose freedom.

steps.title: A piece that cannot move
steps.body: A pin happens when a piece stands between your attacker and a more valuable piece, often the king. If the pinned piece is shielding the king, moving it would be illegal.

steps.title: An absolute pin
steps.body: The bishop on b5 looks through the knight on c6 to the king on e8. The knight cannot legally move.

steps.title: Create the pin
steps.body: Move the bishop from f1 to b5. It will pin the knight on c6 to the king.
steps.successText: The knight is pinned. Capturing it next is often the idea.
steps.errorText: Travel the diagonal from f1 to b5.

steps.title: Can the knight move?
steps.question: The knight on c6 is pinned to the king by the bishop. What is true?

choices.label: The knight can capture the bishop
Moving the knight would expose the king, so it is illegal

steps.successText: That is an absolute pin. Relative pins against a queen are legal, but usually costly.
steps.errorText: Look along the diagonal from the bishop through the knight to the king.

steps.title: Lesson recap
steps.body: Rooks, bishops, and queens create pins. When you see three pieces on a line, ask who is pinned.

lessons.title: Hanging Pieces
lessons.summary: Learn to spot loose material quickly.

steps.title: Hanging means undefended
steps.body: A hanging piece can be captured for free. Most beginner games are decided by one piece left without a defender.

steps.title: The queen is loose
steps.body: Black's queen on d5 has no defender. White's rook looks straight up the d-file.

steps.title: Take the hanging queen
steps.body: Capture the queen with the rook, from d1 to d5.
steps.successText: You won the queen because nothing defended it.
steps.errorText: Move the rook from d1 to d5.

steps.title: Before you grab
steps.question: You see a free pawn. What should you check first?

choices.label: Whether taking it hangs one of your own pieces
Whether you have castled on the opposite wing
The color of the square the pawn sits on

steps.successText: A free pawn is not free if you lose a piece to take it.
steps.errorText: Ask what the opponent can capture after your move.

steps.title: Lesson recap
steps.body: Scan every enemy piece that attacks one of yours. If a piece has no friend defending it, it is hanging.

courses.title: Check and Checkmate
courses.description: Checkmate, stalemate, and simple king hunts.

lessons.title: Checkmate Basics
lessons.summary: Learn the difference between checkmate and stalemate.

steps.title: What is checkmate?
steps.body: Checkmate means the king is in check and there is no legal move to escape. The game ends immediately.

steps.title: A checkmate position
steps.body: Black is in check from the queen and has no legal escape squares.

steps.title: A stalemate position
steps.body: Black is not in check, but has no legal move. That makes it stalemate, not checkmate.

steps.title: What is this position?
steps.question: Look at the board. What is the result?
steps.successText: Correct. Black is not in check, but cannot move.
steps.errorText: Not quite. Check first whether the king is actually in check.

steps.title: Click the trapped king
steps.body: Click the black king in this stalemate position.
steps.successText: Correct. That king has no legal moves.
steps.errorText: Try again. Click the black king on h8.

steps.title: Lesson recap
steps.body: Checkmate wins. Stalemate draws. Always ask: is the king in check or just trapped?

lessons.title: Queen vs King
lessons.summary: Practice shrinking the enemy king's space with the queen.

steps.title: The big idea
steps.body: The queen traps the enemy king by cutting off space. Your king helps finish the job.

steps.title: Start by shrinking the box
steps.body: Do not give random checks forever. First reduce the enemy king's safe area.

steps.title: What should White do first?
steps.question: What is the best practical plan here?

choices.label: Trap the king and bring your king closer

steps.successText: Correct. Restrict first, then bring your king in.
steps.errorText: Not quite. The goal is to shrink the king's space, not just check forever.

steps.title: Make a restricting queen move
steps.body: Move the queen from g2 to g6 to cut off the king without hanging it.
steps.successText: Good. That move cuts the king's space down sharply.
steps.errorText: Try again. Move the queen to g6.

steps.title: After the box shrinks
steps.body: Once the king is boxed in, your king can walk forward and help finish the mate.

steps.title: Lesson recap
steps.body: With queen vs king, shrink the box, bring your king in, and avoid accidental stalemate.

lessons.title: Rook vs King
lessons.summary: Practice cutting off the king and bringing your own king forward.

steps.title: The rook cuts off space
steps.body: A rook wins by fencing the enemy king in. Your king then walks up to help.

steps.title: Think about cutting off the king
steps.body: The rook should reduce the enemy king's space before the final mate.

steps.title: What is White's plan?
steps.question: What should White try to do first?

choices.label: Cut off the king and bring the king in

steps.successText: Correct. Restriction first, then king support.
steps.errorText: Not quite. The rook should reduce the enemy king's space.

steps.title: Cut off the king
steps.body: Move the rook from g2 to g6 to cut the king off without leaving it hanging.
steps.successText: Good. The rook has cut the king off.
steps.errorText: Try again. Move the rook to g6.

steps.title: Now bring your king closer
steps.body: Once the king is boxed in, your own king must help take away the final escape squares.

steps.title: Lesson recap
steps.body: With rook vs king, cut the king off first, then bring your king in to help deliver mate.

courses.title: Practical Play
courses.description: A calm checklist before every move.

lessons.title: Before You Move
lessons.summary: Learn a calm check before you play.

steps.title: Pause for one breath
steps.body: Fast moves lose pieces. Before every move, name the check, the captures, and the threat on the board.

steps.title: A simple checklist
steps.body: Use this list until it becomes a habit.
tasks: Did my opponent leave a piece hanging?
Will my move hang a piece or allow a fork?

steps.title: The tempting pawn
steps.question: You can capture a pawn, but the capture leaves your queen on a square attacked by a rook. What do you do?

choices.label: Take the pawn. Pawns win games.
Save the queen. Material matters more than one pawn.
Move the king for no reason.

steps.successText: Keep the queen. Look for the pawn again after she is safe.
steps.errorText: A queen is worth far more than a pawn.

steps.title: See the danger first
steps.body: The rook on d8 attacks the white queen down the open d-file. Saving the queen comes before any attack.

steps.title: Lesson recap
steps.body: One quiet look prevents most blunders. Checks, captures, threats, then your plan.

lessons.title: Checks, Captures, Threats
lessons.summary: Learn the first questions to ask on every turn.

steps.title: Look in this order
steps.body: Checks come first because they demand an answer. Then captures, especially of undefended pieces. Then threats such as forks and pins.

steps.title: This is check
steps.body: The queen on e2 attacks the king on e1. White must answer the check.

steps.title: Capture the checker
steps.body: The queen is unprotected. Take it with the king, from e1 to e2.
steps.successText: Capturing the checking piece is one of the three ways out of check.
steps.errorText: Move the king from e1 to e2.

steps.title: Step out of check
steps.body: The queen on e3 checks along the file. Move the king to d1 or f1.
steps.successText: Moving the king off the line also escapes check.
steps.errorText: Step to d1 or f1. Both squares are safe.

steps.title: The third way out
steps.question: Besides moving the king or capturing the checker, how else can you escape check from a sliding piece?

choices.label: Block the line with another piece

steps.successText: Interposing works against rooks, bishops, and queens. It does not work against knights.
steps.errorText: Put something in the way of a rook, bishop, or queen.

steps.title: Lesson recap
steps.body: Checks, then captures, then threats. Use that scan on your opponent's move and on the move you are about to play.

lessons.title: Simple Blunder Check
lessons.summary: Learn a short routine to avoid obvious mistakes.

steps.title: One question saves games
steps.body: After the move you want to play, ask: can my opponent checkmate me or win a piece for free? If yes, pick another move.

steps.title: Save the queen
steps.body: The rook on d8 attacks your queen. Move the queen off the d-file, or capture the rook.
steps.successText: The queen is safe. That is the whole lesson.
steps.errorText: Leave the d-file, or capture the rook on d8. Moving the king leaves the queen hanging.

steps.title: What is a blunder?
steps.question: Which move is a blunder?

choices.label: A move that drops a piece or allows mate
Any move that does not give check

steps.successText: Quiet moves are fine. Dropping a piece is not.
steps.errorText: A blunder loses something important. Castling is usually good.

steps.title: Lesson recap
steps.body: You do not need a long combination to improve. Stop hanging pieces, answer checks, and castle.

openings.name: English Opening
openings.description: A flexible flank-opening course that teaches positional play, center control from the side, and calm development.
ideas: Control d5 indirectly with c4.
Stay flexible before committing central pawns.
Develop naturally and avoid rushing attacks.
The English controls the center from the side, then develops quietly before choosing a central break.
Trade only when it improves your position, removes danger, or opens a useful file.
By move 8-12, you should know your early middlegame plan: safe king, active pieces, and one central break.
commonMistakes: Treating c4 like a gambit trick.
Ignoring development because the center is quiet.
Pushing too many pawns before pieces are out.
Stopping after memorized moves and playing without a plan.
Trading automatically without asking what improves afterward.
Starting an attack before castling or finishing development.

moves.title: Control d5
moves.explanation: c4 fights for d5 from the side and keeps the center flexible. c4 changes the central structure. Central pawn moves should either claim space, challenge an enemy pawn, or open a line for a piece. The English controls the center from the side, then develops quietly before choosing a central break.

moves.title: Black takes space
moves.explanation: Black occupies the center directly. e5 changes the central structure. Central pawn moves should either claim space, challenge an enemy pawn, or open a line for a piece. The English controls the center from the side, then develops quietly before choosing a central break.

moves.title: Develop toward d5
moves.explanation: Nc3 develops and increases control over d5. White can choose the center structure later. Nc3 develops a knight to c3. Developed pieces control central squares, help castling, and make future tactics possible without forcing anything too early.

moves.title: Develop to f6
moves.explanation: Nf6 develops a knight to f6. Developed pieces control central squares, help castling, and make future tactics possible without forcing anything too early.

moves.title: Improve with g3
moves.explanation: g3 is a practical improving move for White. In real games, keep asking: is my king safe, are my pieces active, and what central pawn break comes next?

moves.title: Develop to g2

moves.title: Get the king safe
moves.explanation: O-O moves the king to safety and brings the rook closer to the center. This is usually the moment when the opening becomes an early middlegame plan: The English controls the center from the side, then develops quietly before choosing a central break.

moves.title: Get the king safe
moves.explanation: O-O gets the king safe and brings a rook closer to the center. This is the bridge from opening to middlegame: now look for your worst piece, your safest trade, and your best pawn break.

moves.title: Develop to e6
moves.explanation: Be6 improves a piece and adds control over important squares. Developed pieces create threats naturally, so you do not need to force an attack before castling.
